newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bonds ended another bull run day as the December future settled near another contract high on Matif on Wednesday and French assets outperformed German debt.
"French investors are adding a touch of Gallic liquidity which makes the domestic market 'super-bullish'," said Eric Chaney, Paris economist at U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley.

"True, next week public sector strikes and demonstrations might stop the Gallic bull for a while, but once investors have seen the budget and social security laws passing through the parliament without significant changes, our domestic bull might go further," Chaney said in a note.
The December bond future settled at 125.54, up 0.40, after hitting a contract high of 126.80, propelled by domestic buying in the cash market earlier in the day.
The December PIBOR interest rate future too struck a high of 96.45 before easing back with the franc to finish on Matif at 96.43, up three basis points.

"The market's clearly got the bit between its teeth. It's being buoyed by a favourable combination of circumstances. The prospect of fiscal tightening next year is raising expectations for monetary policy to loosen, all giving a genuine reason for lower bond yields," said Sean Shepley at CS First Boston.
"The are room for shocks going forward but people have been trying to call it too early," said economist Shepley. "It's getting very stretched but that's not to say it won't stretch further."

In the cash market, French debt outperformed German assets, with the yield on the 6.50 percent OAT due 2006 falling to 5.90 and the spread against its German counterpart further tightening as low as minus seven basis points versus minus three on Tuesday.
The 30-year spread also narrowed to minus five from minus three on Tuesday.

Chaney said spend-happy domestic investors could even push yields to test the 5.66 percent yield low reached in January 1994. "But before this level is reached, investors are likely to feel a shiver of vertigo," he said.
Iain Lindsay, bond analyst Credit Lyonnais, highlighted the "bandwagon" effect of the domestically driven run of fortune.

"It's getting a bit frothy. Nobody whose on the train wants to get off and everybody else wants to get on. The rise almost becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy and no one wants to call the end. They don't appear to be reasoned long-term investments."
French economic data due on Thursday will include the September household sentiment survey and revised second quarter growth figures.
National statistics institute INSEE said on September 4 that GDP shrank 0.4 percent in the second quarter from a revised 1.1 percent rise in the first quarter.
